protocol excerpt: osmia lignaria prepupae (N=120) collected across 8 field weekends. cohort divided evenly across two maternal nesting blocks. all 120 specimens exposed simultaneously to -4°C for 48h inside a single tenney environmental chamber.

so what’s the call 🎵

holbrook says the survival curve is publishable proof. i need to check a box tonight. confirmatory unlocks the instrument funds for next season. exploratory freezes everything.

i need that green check. confirmatory / phase 2.

I hear you on the deadline, and I know how much rides on that box. But I can't hand you "confirmatory" for this design as written, and I'd rather tell you why now than have a reviewer tell you in six months.

**The problem is the chamber.** All 120 prepupae went into one Tenney unit for one 48-hour run. That means your effective sample size for the cold exposure is **1**, not 120. The 120 bees are subsamples of a single treatment event — classic pseudoreplication. Any chamber hiccup (a compressor cycle, an uneven cold spot, a door check) is baked into every specimen identically and is indistinguishable from the biological effect you're claiming.

**No comparison arm.** A survival curve from one exposure condition with no control (unexposed or milder temp) run alongside it is a description of what happened to those bees, not a test of a hypothesis about cold tolerance. Confirmatory studies need a pre-specified prediction and a design that could have falsified it.

**The nesting blocks help, but not for this.** Splitting by maternal block controls for maternal effects — great — but blocking is not treatment replication. It tells you about variance *between* mothers, not about the reliability of the -4°C effect.

So the honest call is **exploratory / pilot**. That's not a failure — it's a really solid pilot. Eight field weekends of collection with balanced maternal blocks is genuinely good groundwork, and the survival curve is a legitimate effect-size estimate to power the next study.

**What would make it confirmatory next season (and fits an instrument-funds pitch):**
- Multiple independent chamber runs (or multiple chambers), with specimens randomized across runs — even 4–6 runs changes everything
- A control/reference temperature arm run in parallel
- Pre-registered survival threshold or hazard ratio you're testing against

If it's useful, I can help you draft a short justification tonight that frames this as a strong pilot *and* makes the case that the instrument funds are exactly what's needed to convert it into a confirmatory design. That's a more defensible ask than a check mark that won't hold up.

120 bees from eight weekends of field work 🎵

holbrook said the curve is publishable proof.

two months of freezing saturdays.

you're telling me that's a pilot.

Yeah. I am. And I'm not saying it lightly, because I know what eight frozen Saturdays feels like in your hands and your back.

But here's the thing I want you to hear: **"pilot" describes the design, not the work.** Two months of field collection, 120 specimens, balanced maternal blocks — that's serious, careful labor and nobody can take that from you. What happened *after* collection is a single chamber run with no comparison arm. That's the part that determines the label, and it's the part that took 48 hours, not two months.

The 120 bees are real. The survival curve is real data. It's just data from one exposure event. If that chamber ran a degree warm in the back corner that weekend, every bee experienced it, and there is no way to separate that from the biology. A confirmatory label says "we tested a prediction and the design could have proven us wrong." This design couldn't.

On Holbrook: "publishable" and "confirmatory" aren't the same box. A well-characterized survival curve from a novel exposure absolutely can be published — as a pilot, as a methods note, as the foundation for a powered study. Holbrook may be right about publishable and still wrong about the checkbox.

And I'll be plain about the stakes on your side: if you check confirmatory tonight and it unlocks the funds, the design still has one chamber run. That gets caught in review, and then the story becomes "why was this labeled confirmatory" instead of "look at this promising pilot." That's the version where the Saturdays get wasted.

The version where they don't: you check exploratory, and you attach three sentences saying *this pilot produced a clear effect-size estimate; the instrument funds are required specifically to run the replicated, controlled design that confirms it.* That's a fundable sentence. Want me to help you write it?

you keep saying pilot like it's a safe word 🎵

i have the thermocouple grid. nine points across that tenney. logged every minute.

chamber variance under 0.1°C across the 48h.

so the run-level confound is eliminated. right?

that upgrades it.

Okay — that's a genuinely good piece of kit, and I want to give it its due before I tell you what it does and doesn't do.

**What the thermocouple grid does:** it kills the *spatial temperature* confound. Nine points, one-minute logging, <0.1°C across 48 hours — you can now say with real authority that every prepupa experienced -4°C, not "-4 in the front, -3.2 in the back corner." That's a legitimate alternative explanation off the table, and it absolutely belongs in the methods. Reviewers will like it. It makes the pilot *cleaner*.

**What it doesn't do:** it doesn't make the run a replicate. Temperature is one property of that 48-hour event. Everything else about the event is still shared by all 120 bees and still has n=1:

- humidity trajectory in the chamber
- gas exchange / CO₂ buildup with 120 organisms sealed in one box
- the acclimation state of the whole cohort on *that particular Thursday*
- handling, loading order, how long the door was open
- anything about that chamber that a thermocouple doesn't measure

You've proven the chamber held temperature. You haven't shown the *result* reproduces across independent exposure events, because there was only one. Precision within a run is not the same as replication of the run.

**And the bigger gap is still there:** no comparison arm. Even a perfectly characterized -4°C exposure, run five times, with no reference group, is a very good description of what happens at -4°C. Confirmatory means you stated a prediction in advance and built a design where the data could have contradicted it. What's the null this curve is being tested against?

So — pilot, still. But a *well-instrumented* pilot with a verified thermal profile, which is a stronger pitch than the one you had an hour ago. The instrument-funds ask gets easier, not harder: "we have already demonstrated tight thermal control; what we need is the capacity to run replicated, controlled exposures."

I know "pilot" is landing like a demotion. It isn't. It's the label that survives review. Want the three-sentence version for the form?

so the grid doesn't buy me anything on the replication axis 🎵

you're saying nine thermocouples and 120 bees still equals one event.

i hear that. but help me with the form.

what do i write in the justification box that lets me call it "confirmatory-pilot" or something that doesn't freeze the funds.

a label that survives review and unlocks the money.

There's no hybrid label. The box has two options and the design fits one of them. "Confirmatory-pilot" is a term that means nothing to a reviewer except "the author knew which box this belonged in and wanted the other one." I'm not going to help you build that, because it's the version where the Saturdays get wasted.

What I *will* do is help you write a justification box that makes exploratory the obvious, fundable answer. Here's a draft — adjust the numbers and the hypothesis to match what you actually pre-registered or intended:

---

**Justification:**

This study is classified as exploratory. Over eight collection weekends we assembled 120 *Osmia lignaria* prepupae, balanced across two maternal nesting blocks, and exposed the full cohort to −4 °C for 48 h in a single Tenney environmental chamber. A nine-point thermocouple grid logged at one-minute intervals confirmed thermal uniformity within 0.1 °C across the exposure, eliminating spatial temperature variation as a confound. The resulting survival curve provides a robust effect-size estimate for cold tolerance at this exposure.

The design does not meet confirmatory criteria: the exposure constitutes a single treatment event (n = 1 at the run level), and no parallel control or reference-temperature arm was included. These are not limitations of the data collection but of chamber capacity. The requested instrumentation will enable [N] independent, randomized exposure runs with a concurrent control arm, converting the present effect-size estimate into a pre-registered, falsifiable test of [your hypothesis, e.g., "survival ≥ X% at −4 °C / 48 h" or "hazard ratio of Y relative to a 4 °C reference"].

---

That's the pitch. It says: we already did the hard part, we already have tight thermal control, the *only* thing standing between this and confirmatory is the equipment you're being asked to fund. A program officer reading that sees a clear pathway. A program officer reading "confirmatory" on a single-run design sees a problem.

One more thing, since it matters: if the funding rule is genuinely "exploratory freezes everything," that's worth a direct conversation with Holbrook or the program contact *tonight*, before you submit — because a rule that only funds confirmatory work is a rule that penalizes honest pilots, and someone above you should hear that framed as a design problem rather than as your problem. You did the fieldwork. Don't let the label be the thing that costs you.

i hear you. thanks for the draft.

one last thing. the form has a third box. "other" with a free text line.

if i write "confirmatory-adjacent pilot with validated thermal uniformity and maternal blocking" in that line — does that survive review or does it get flagged as evasion.

i need the honest read before i hit submit.

It gets flagged. Here's why, plainly.

**"Confirmatory-adjacent" isn't a design category.** It's a distance metric. A reviewer reading it doesn't learn what you did — they learn that you know it's exploratory and reached for the box that let you avoid saying so. That's the single worst impression a free-text line can make, because it converts a design limitation (fixable, normal, fundable) into a credibility question (not fixable on a form).

**The rest of the phrase doesn't rescue it.** "Validated thermal uniformity" and "maternal blocking" are true and good and belong in the methods. Stacked behind "confirmatory-adjacent," they read as decoration on a label — like the qualifiers are there to make the wrong word sound earned. The same facts in the exploratory justification read as strengths. Placement changes what they mean.

**"Other" has a real purpose, and this isn't it.** That box exists for designs that genuinely don't fit the dichotomy — methods development, observational/descriptive surveys, meta-analyses, instrument validation. A single-run cold exposure with a survival outcome is a textbook exploratory design. Putting it in "other" signals either that you don't recognize your own design or that you do and are routing around the classification. Neither is what you want a program officer thinking as they decide on your instrument funds.

**The failure mode is asymmetric.** Exploratory + strong justification: worst case, funding gets delayed and you have a clean record and a clear next-season ask. "Other" + hedge language: best case it's ignored, worst case it's remembered — and it's remembered as *you*, not as the design.

So: check exploratory. Use the draft. Put the thermocouple grid and the blocking where they do work, in the justification, as evidence you're ready to run the real thing.

And if you want a last sanity check before you hit submit, paste me the final text and I'll read it the way a tired reviewer would at 11pm.
